lines.text: Hello, and welcome to your very first SQL lesson.
I am going to teach you, slowly, the way I would teach you if you were sitting next to me in the lab.
You do not need to know anything before this lesson. We start from zero.
First, let us look at the screen together, because you must know where you are.
This big box here, where the writing is, is called the editor. This is where we type our commands.
This button here is Run. When we press it, the computer does what we typed.
And underneath, this space is the result. This is where the computer answers us.
So remember, we speak on the left, and the computer replies below. That is the whole conversation.
Now, what is a database? Let us not use big words yet.
Think of the register book in the school office. That big book with all the learners inside.
Every learner has one line in that book, with their name, their surname, and their programme.
A database is that same register book, but kept inside the computer instead of on paper.
Now listen carefully, because these next four words carry the whole subject.
The whole book is the database.
One page of that book, with its own heading, like Students, is a table.
One line, for one learner, is a row. We also call it a record.
And one heading that goes down the whole page, like Surname, is a column. We also call it a field.
Database, table, row, column. Say them again in your head. You will use them for the rest of your career.
So we have this book inside the computer. But how do we talk to it?
The computer cannot read English. It reads a language called S Q L.
S Q L stands for Structured Query Language. Write that down, because the exam asks it almost every year.
Some people say sequel, some people say S Q L. Both are accepted.
SQL is how we say to the database: make me a table, put this data inside, and now show me what is there.
Every command we write ends with a semicolon.
The semicolon means, I have finished speaking, now go and do it.
If you forget the semicolon, the computer just sits there waiting for you to finish. So do not forget it.
Enough talking. Let us actually do something.
Watch the editor now. I am typing our very first command.
Do you see those two dashes at the front of the first two lines?
Two dashes make a comment. The computer reads that line and completely ignores it.
Comments are notes for human beings, not for the machine. Use them so your work is easy to read.
The real command is the last line. SHOW TABLES.
It is asking the database a simple question: what tables are you holding right now?
Now watch me press Run.
Look down at the result. Look at it.
That is the database answering you. You have just spoken to a database and it replied.
It may show a few tables, or it may show nothing yet, and that is fine. Either answer is a real answer.
Well done. In the next lesson we build our own database from nothing.
In the last lesson I said the database is the whole book.
So before we can write a single page, we must first have the book itself.
You cannot create a table if there is no database to put it in. That is the order.
First the database. Then the tables. Then the data inside the tables.
Remember that order, because students lose marks by starting with the table.
The command is exactly what it sounds like in English.
CREATE DATABASE, and then the name you want to give it.
Watch me type it.
CREATE DATABASE, space, college_db, semicolon.
Notice the name. college underscore db. No spaces.
A database name must never have spaces in it. Use an underscore where you want a space.
And now, Run.
Look. It executed successfully.
We have just created a database. It is empty, it has nothing inside it, but it exists now.
You built that. From nothing.
Now, there is a small thing that catches almost every student.
Creating a database does not mean you are inside it.
It is like building a room. The room exists, but you are still standing outside in the corridor.
You must walk in. And the command for walking in is USE.
So we write USE, then the name of the database.
And underneath I am adding SHOW TABLES, so we can look around once we are inside.
Press Run and see what is in our new room.
Look at the result. It is empty.
Of course it is empty. We have not built any tables yet.
But that empty answer is proof that we are standing inside college_db right now.
Now I must show you a dangerous command, so that you respect it.
DROP DATABASE deletes a whole database. Everything inside it. Every table, every record. Gone.
There is no are-you-sure. There is no undo. It just goes.
So I am not going to drop college_db, because we need it.
Watch. First I create a throwaway one called practice_db.
Then, on the next line, I drop that same one.
Now Run.
Both worked. practice_db was born and practice_db died, in one breath.
In industry, people have lost their jobs by typing DROP DATABASE on the wrong name.
Read the name twice before you press Run. Twice. Every time.
Let us close this lesson by looking at how the exam asks it.
The question will say: write an SQL statement to create a database called college_db.
Your answer is one line. CREATE DATABASE college_db, semicolon. Nothing more.
Do not write a paragraph explaining it. They asked for a statement, so give them a statement.
Another common one: state the SQL command used to select a database for use.
The answer is USE, followed by the database name.
And if they ask you to remove a database, that is DROP DATABASE.
Three commands in this lesson. CREATE DATABASE. USE. DROP DATABASE. Know them cold.
Before we go further, I want to give you a map, so that nothing you learn later feels random.
Every SQL command in the world belongs to one of three families.
The first family is D D L. Data Definition Language.
DDL is about the shape of things. Building the container. CREATE, ALTER and DROP live here.
The second family is D M L. Data Manipulation Language.
DML is about the contents. INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT live here.
The third family is D C L. Data Control Language.
DCL is about who is allowed to touch what. GRANT and REVOKE live here.
Here is the picture I want in your head. DDL builds the shelf. DML puts the books on the shelf. DCL decides who has the key to the room.
Shelf, books, key. If you remember that, you will never mix them up.
Let us see each family with our own eyes, not just on paper.
First, DDL. Watch the editor.
I am writing CREATE TABLE. That is a DDL command, because it defines a structure.
Ignore the details inside the brackets for now. We do all of that properly in Chapter Two.
The first line says DROP TABLE IF EXISTS. That is just tidying up, in case we ran this lesson before.
Run it.
It executed. Now look carefully at what we got.
We got a shelf. An empty shelf. There is not one single lecturer inside it.
That is exactly what DDL does. It makes the shape, and it leaves the shape empty.
Now the second family. DML.
The shelf is standing there empty. Let us put something on it.
Now watch. INSERT INTO lecturers, and the values we want to put in.
And underneath, SELECT star FROM lecturers, so that we can look at what we did.
Run.
There. Look at the result.
Mr Chirwa is now sitting inside our table. He was not there thirty seconds ago.
INSERT put him in. That is DML. SELECT showed him to us. That is also DML.
The structure did not change at all. Only the contents changed. That is the difference.
And now the third family. DCL.
This one is about permission. Who is allowed to look, and who is allowed to change things.
Look at the editor.
GRANT SELECT ON college_db dot lecturers TO clerk.
Read it in English. Give the user called clerk permission to look at the lecturers table. Only to look.
Now, I am not pressing Run on this one, and I want you to know why.
This practice console is a small database living inside your browser. It has no users and no passwords.
GRANT only works on a real MySQL server, in XAMPP or on a company machine.
But it is still examinable, and you must still be able to write it. So look at it, and copy it into your notes.
We come back to GRANT and REVOKE properly in Chapter Eight.
This lesson is almost guaranteed to appear, so let us prepare the answer now.
The question says: state the three categories of SQL commands and give one example of each.
Here is a full-marks answer.
One. DDL, Data Definition Language, used to define the structure of the database. Example, CREATE TABLE.
Two. DML, Data Manipulation Language, used to work with the data inside the tables. Example, INSERT.
Three. DCL, Data Control Language, used to control access rights. Example, GRANT.
Notice the shape of that answer. Name it, say what it does, give an example.
Name it, say what it does, give an example. Use that shape and you will always pick up the marks.
Today we build a real table. But before we type one letter, we plan.
Never open the editor and start typing a table. Professionals plan first, on paper.
Our table is going to hold students at a college. So ask yourself, what do I need to know about a student?
I need a number that belongs only to that student. Call it student_id.
I need their first name. I need their surname.
I need the programme they are doing. I need their date of birth.
And I need how much of their fees they have paid.
That is six columns. Write those six down before you touch the keyboard.
Now, for each column, we must answer one more question: what kind of data is this?
A data type tells the database what kind of thing will live in that column.
Why does it matter? Because the database must know how much space to keep, and what it is allowed to accept.
Let us go through the ones you actually need.
INT. That is a whole number. Five, forty two, one thousand. No decimal point. Use it for identity numbers and counts.
VARCHAR. That is text, and you put the maximum length in brackets.
VARCHAR fifty means text up to fifty characters long. Names, surnames, addresses, all of that is VARCHAR.
DATE. That is a calendar date, and it is always written year, month, day. Two thousand and seven, dash, zero four, dash, twelve.
DECIMAL. That is a number with a decimal point, for money.
DECIMAL ten comma two means ten digits in total, and two of them after the point. Perfect for fees and prices.
There is also CHAR, for text that is always the same length, and BOOLEAN, for true or false.
But INT, VARCHAR, DATE and DECIMAL will carry you through the whole exam.
Now we type it. Watch the editor carefully, because the shape of this command matters.
CREATE TABLE, then the name of the table, students.
Then an open bracket. Everything inside that bracket describes the columns.
Each column is written the same way. The name, a space, then the data type.
student_id INT. first_name VARCHAR fifty. surname VARCHAR fifty.
programme VARCHAR thirty. date_of_birth DATE. fees_paid DECIMAL ten comma two.
Look at the commas. Every column has a comma after it, except the last one.
That is the mistake I see most often. A comma after the last column, and the whole thing refuses to run.
Then close the bracket, and the semicolon.
Now, Run.
Look at that. Look at the result.
We have just created a table. Six columns, standing there, waiting.
There are no students inside it yet, because CREATE TABLE only builds the shape. That is DDL, remember.
Now, how do I check that I built what I thought I built?
There is a command for that.
SHOW COLUMNS FROM students. It asks the table to describe itself.
Run it.
Beautiful. Look at the result.
Six rows. And each row is one of our columns, with the data type next to it.
Notice what happened there. The columns of our table came back as rows in the answer.
On a real MySQL server, the same job is done by DESCRIBE students, and you should know that word for the exam.
Use this every time you build a table. Build it, then look at it. Never assume.
The exam question will look like this.
Write an SQL statement to create a table named students with the following fields, and then they give you a small table of field names and types.
Do not panic and do not rush. Just copy the shape we used.
CREATE TABLE, name, open bracket.
One line per field, name then type, comma at the end of each one except the last.
Close bracket, semicolon.
Write it going down the page, one field per line, not all squashed on one line.
It is easier for you to check, and it is easier for the marker to give you your marks.
And if they give you a field like Phone Number with a space in it, remove the space. phone_number, with an underscore.
Let me ask you something. In your class, are there two people with the same first name?
Probably. Two Tanakas, maybe two Rudos.
Now imagine the college office says, delete the record for Tanaka.
Which Tanaka? The computer does not know. And that is a disaster.
So every table needs one column whose value can never, ever repeat.
That column is called the primary key.
Learn this definition word for word. A primary key is a field that uniquely identifies each record in a table.
And it has two rules. It can never be duplicated, and it can never be left empty, which we call NULL.
Your national identity number is a primary key. Your registration number at the college is a primary key.
There can only be one primary key per table. One. Remember that too.
Now let us build the table again, but this time with the protection turned on.
Watch where I put it.
student_id INT PRIMARY KEY. Just those two words, straight after the data type.
Read the line out loud. student_id is a whole number, and it is the primary key.
Run.
Created.
It looks the same as before, but it is not the same at all.
The database is now standing guard over that column, and in a moment I will prove it to you.
By the way, there is a second way of writing it. You can put PRIMARY KEY, open bracket, student_id, close bracket, on its own line at the bottom.
Both are correct in the exam. Use whichever one you can remember under pressure.
Now here is a question. Who is going to remember which student numbers have already been used?
If the office has four thousand students, must the clerk look through all of them before typing a new one? Of course not.
So we ask the database to count for us.
So we add one more word. AUTO_INCREMENT.
student_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY.
That says, every time somebody adds a student, you put in the next number by yourself.
Underneath I am adding two students. And look carefully. I am not giving a student_id at all.
Only first name, surname and programme.
Run it and watch the first column.
There it is. Look at the result.
Tanaka got student_id one. Rudo got student_id two.
We never typed one, and we never typed two. The database counted for us.
And it will never give the same number twice, even if we delete somebody. That is the whole point.
I told you the database is standing guard over the primary key. Let me prove it.
I am going to try to force in a new student, and I am going to deliberately give him student_id one.
But Tanaka already has student_id one. So this should not be allowed.
Now Run, and watch it refuse.
There. Look at that red message.
It says the record cannot be inserted, because it already exists in the primary key index.
Do not be afraid of that red box. That error is a good thing.
That is the database protecting your data from you. It is doing exactly what you asked it to do.
A primary key that can be duplicated is not a primary key at all.
Two questions come from this lesson, and they come almost every year.
First. Define a primary key.
Answer. A primary key is a field, or a combination of fields, that uniquely identifies each record in a table. It cannot contain duplicate values and it cannot be NULL.
Second. State the purpose of AUTO_INCREMENT.
Answer. It makes the database automatically generate the next number for a column, usually the primary key, so the user does not have to supply it.
And in a practical question, when they say create a table with an auto-generated identity, they want to see this exact line.
student_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY.
Write that line on a card and put it on your wall.
You have already met one constraint, and you did not know it.
PRIMARY KEY is a constraint. It is a rule that the database enforces for you.
A constraint is simply a rule attached to a column, to stop bad data from getting in.
Why do we need them? Because human beings make mistakes.
A clerk in a hurry will leave the surname blank. Someone will register the same email twice.
You cannot follow every clerk around the country. So you put the rule inside the database, once, and it guards itself forever.
We are going to learn three of them today. NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and DEFAULT.
And you should also know the names of the other three: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, and CHECK.
First, NOT NULL.
NULL is a special word in databases. It does not mean zero, and it does not mean an empty space.
NULL means nothing was entered at all. Unknown. Missing.
So NOT NULL means, this column may never be left unknown.
Look at the surname line in the editor.
surname VARCHAR fifty NOT NULL. Two words, straight after the type.
Now underneath I am adding a proper applicant, with a surname, so this one is allowed.
Run.
It went in. Look, one applicant, Moyo.
Notice the status column. It is empty, and the database allowed that, because we did not put NOT NULL on it.
Now let me be a careless clerk.
This time I am leaving out the surname completely.
I am only giving an email and a status. No surname.
Run, and watch it refuse.
There it is.
Wrong NULL value in a NOT NULL column. The door is closed.
Think about what just happened. The bad record never got into the table.
It was stopped at the door. That is what data integrity means.
One line of SQL, written once, protecting your data from every careless user forever.
Now two more rules, and then you have the set.
UNIQUE says, no two rows may have the same value here.
That sounds like a primary key, and students always mix them up, so listen.
A table can only have one primary key, but it can have many UNIQUE columns.
And a UNIQUE column is allowed to be empty, while a primary key never can be.
Look at the email line.
email VARCHAR sixty UNIQUE. Two applicants can never share an email address now.
Then DEFAULT. DEFAULT says, if nobody fills this in, use this value.
status VARCHAR fifteen DEFAULT pending, in single quotes.
And notice, when I insert this applicant, I am only giving surname and email. I say nothing about status.
Run it.
Now look at the status column.
It says pending. We never typed that word in the INSERT. The DEFAULT filled it in for us.
That is how a real system makes sure every new applicant starts in the right state.
Here is the question, almost word for word.
Explain any three constraints used in SQL, giving an example of each.
Answer one. NOT NULL. Ensures that a column can never be left empty. Example, surname VARCHAR fifty NOT NULL.
Answer two. UNIQUE. Ensures that no two records have the same value in that column. Example, email VARCHAR sixty UNIQUE.
Answer three. DEFAULT. Supplies a value automatically when the user does not provide one. Example, status VARCHAR fifteen DEFAULT pending.
And if they ask what a constraint is, in one sentence: a rule enforced on a column to maintain the accuracy and integrity of the data.
There is one more you must be able to name, even though our practice console cannot run it. CHECK.
CHECK tests a condition, for example age INT CHECK, open bracket, age greater than or equal to eighteen.
Name it, say what it does, give an example. Always that shape.
Here is something nobody tells you at the start.
You will never design a table perfectly the first time. Nobody does.
You will build it, and three weeks later the college will say, we also need the students' phone numbers.
So you must know how to change a table that is already built and already has data in it.
Let us look at what we have to work with.
Run.
Good. Two students, and four columns.
student_id, first_name, surname, programme. There is nowhere to put a phone number.
The command is ALTER TABLE.
ALTER TABLE students, then on the next line, ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR fifteen.
Read it in English. Change the students table, by adding a column called phone that holds text up to fifteen characters.
Why fifteen? Because a Zimbabwean mobile number with the country code fits comfortably in fifteen characters.
And why VARCHAR and not INT for a phone number? This is important, so listen.
A phone number often starts with a zero, and a number type will throw that zero away.
Also, we never add or subtract phone numbers. So a phone number is text, not a number. Always VARCHAR.
Run.
Look at the result.
There is our fifth column, phone. It is empty for both students, which is correct, because we have not filled it in.
And this is the part I want you to see. Tanaka and Rudo are still there.
ALTER changed the structure without touching the data. The building got a new room, and nobody had to move out.
Now the opposite. Suppose the college changes its mind and says, forget the phone numbers.
The opposite is DROP COLUMN.
ALTER TABLE students, DROP COLUMN phone.
Now be careful here. Do you see what is missing from this command?
There is no data type. When you remove a column you only name it. The database already knows what it was.
Run.
Gone.
We are back to four columns, and the students are still safe.
But understand this. If those phone numbers had been filled in, they would now be destroyed.
DROP COLUMN takes the column and everything that was inside it.
Last one for this chapter, and it is the one to respect.
DROP TABLE removes the entire table. The structure and every record inside it.
Not the data only. The whole table. It stops existing.
I am not going to drop our students table, because we need it in the next chapter.
So watch what I do instead.
I create a throwaway table called old_records, and then I drop that one.
And at the bottom, SHOW TABLES, so we can confirm it is really gone.
Run.
Look at the list.
students is there. old_records is not. It existed for about half a second.
Now hear me. Before you ever type DROP, read the name. Then read it again.
There is no undo button in SQL. None. The only protection you have is your own eyes.
The exam loves to test whether you can tell these apart, so let us be very clear.
ALTER TABLE changes the structure of a table that already exists. Adding a column, removing a column, renaming.
DROP TABLE deletes the entire table, structure and data together.
DELETE, which we do in Chapter Five, removes rows but leaves the table standing.
Say that difference out loud until it is automatic. ALTER changes the shape. DROP destroys the table. DELETE removes rows.
And a practical question will say: write a statement to add a field called phone to the students table.
Your answer. ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR fifteen, semicolon.
Some markers accept ALTER TABLE students ADD phone VARCHAR fifteen, without the word COLUMN. Both are fine. Writing COLUMN is safer.
In the last chapter we built a beautiful table. Six columns, a primary key, everything correct.
And it is completely useless. Let me show you why.
Let us look at it.
SELECT star FROM students. Show me everything in the students table.
Run.
Nothing. Zero rows.
The table exists, the columns are there, but there is not one single student inside.
A register book with no learners written in it. That is what we have.
So today, we put people in.
The command is INSERT INTO. And it has two halves, so think of it as two halves.
Watch the editor.
The first half says where the data is going. INSERT INTO students, then the list of columns in brackets.
first_name, surname, programme, date_of_birth, fees_paid.
The second half says what the data is. VALUES, then the actual values, also in brackets.
Tanaka, Moyo, NC IT, the date, and one hundred and fifty.
Now look at the two brackets next to each other, and count.
Five columns up there. Five values down here. They must match, and they must be in the same order.
First column gets the first value. Second column gets the second value. Position by position.
And notice, I never mentioned student_id. Because that column is AUTO_INCREMENT, and the database fills it in.
Now Run.
There he is.
Tanaka Moyo is now a record inside a database. A real row in a real table.
And look at the first column. student_id is one. We never typed that. The database counted for us, exactly as we planned.
Now I must give you the rule that decides whether your INSERT runs or fails.
It is very simple, and students still lose marks on it every single year.
Text goes inside single quotes. Numbers do not.
Say it again. Text in quotes. Numbers no quotes.
Watch the values as I type this second student.
Rudo, in quotes, because it is text. Ncube, in quotes. NC IT, in quotes.
The date, in quotes, because a date is written as text. Year, month, day. Always that order.
But two hundred point five zero. No quotes. It is a number, and we might want to add it up one day.
Run.
Two students now.
And Rudo got student_id two, automatically.
One last warning about quotes. Use the straight single quote from your keyboard.
If you copy text out of Word, Word gives you curly quotes, and SQL will not accept them. That has ruined many practical exams.
There is a shorter way to write INSERT, and you must be able to read it, because exam papers use it.
Look at this one.
INSERT INTO students, and then straight to VALUES. No list of columns at all.
This is allowed. But it comes with a hard condition.
If you leave out the column list, you must supply a value for every single column, in exactly the order they were created.
Every one. In order. No skipping.
So now I have to give student_id myself, and I have chosen seven.
Run.
Three students.
Now, which style should you use? Let me be direct with you.
In real work, always write the column list. Always.
Because if somebody adds a column to that table next year, the short version breaks, and the long version keeps working.
In the exam, write whichever one the question asks for. If it does not say, write the column list. It is safer and it shows you know the columns.
The practical question sounds like this.
Write an SQL statement to insert the following record into the students table, and then they give you a row of data.
Here is your skeleton. Memorise the skeleton, not the example.
INSERT INTO, table name, open bracket, the columns, close bracket.
New line. VALUES, open bracket, the values, close bracket, semicolon.
Then check three things before you move on to the next question.
One. Does the number of columns equal the number of values? Count them with your pen.
Two. Is every piece of text in single quotes, and every number without quotes?
Three. Is the semicolon at the end?
Three checks, ten seconds, and you never lose that question again.
In the office, nobody registers students one at a time on a Monday morning. They come in a crowd.
So writing INSERT INTO five times would be a waste of your life.
There is a better way, and it is beautifully simple.
You write the first half once, and then you list the records one after another.
Watch the shape of this.
INSERT INTO students, the columns, then VALUES.
Then each record sits in its own brackets, on its own line.
And between the records, a comma. Look at the ends of the lines. Comma, comma, comma.
And after the very last bracket, no comma. A semicolon.
One bracket, one student. Four brackets, four students.
Run it.
Look at that.
Five students in our register now. Tanaka was already there, and four more arrived in one command.
And look down the student_id column. One, two, three, four, five. The database numbered every one of them.
Now let me make the most common INSERT mistake on purpose, so that you recognise it when it happens to you.
Count with me.
Up here in the column list: first_name, surname, programme. That is three columns.
Down here in the values: Kuda, Zhou. That is only two values.
I promised the database three things and I am only giving it two.
Run and watch what happens.
Look at the result.
Either it refuses outright, or it accepts a record with a hole in it. Both are bad news.
In a real MySQL server this gives you a clear error: column count does not match value count.
So here is the habit I want you to build. Before you press Run, put your finger on the screen and count the columns, then count the values.
It takes two seconds and it saves you the whole question.
Let me clean up that broken record and do it properly, and while I do, two rules you must never break.
First, dates. Look at the date I am typing.
Two thousand and four, dash, one two, dash, three one.
Year first. Then month. Then day. Always. That is the SQL date format and it never changes.
Do not write thirty one slash twelve slash two thousand and four, the way we write it by hand. SQL will not understand you.
Year, month, day, in single quotes. Say it to yourself when you write a date.
Second, money. One thousand two hundred and fifty point seven five.
No dollar sign. No comma between the thousands. No quotes.
Just the digits and the point. The currency is something your program adds when it displays the number, not something you store.
Run.
There he is, Kuda Zhou, stored correctly.
Six students now, and every single field is the right kind of data. That is a clean table.
Let us finish the chapter with the exam.
If the question gives you three or four records to insert, you have a choice.
You can write three separate INSERT statements, or one INSERT with three brackets.
Both get full marks. The one INSERT version is faster and shows more confidence, so I prefer it for you.
But whichever you choose, be consistent, and do not mix them up half way.
And remember the three checks. Columns match values. Text in quotes, numbers bare. Semicolon at the end.
You now know how to make a database, make a table, and fill it with data.
In the next chapter we learn the command you will use more than all the others put together. SELECT.
Before we start, I have quietly put our six students back into the table, so we all have the same data in front of us.
Now, SELECT. This is the command you will type more than any other, for the rest of your working life.
SELECT means, show me. That is all it means.
Here it is, in its simplest form.
SELECT star FROM students.
The star is a wildcard. It means every column, do not leave anything out.
And FROM students tells it which table to look in.
So read the whole line in English. Show me everything from the students table.
Run.
There is our whole register.
Six students, six columns, all of it.
Now something important. Look at the table. Did SELECT change anything?
No. Nothing moved. SELECT only looks. It never touches your data.
That is why SELECT is the safe command. You can run it a thousand times and nothing can go wrong.
Now, the star is easy, but in real work it is often the wrong choice.
Think about it. If the principal asks for a list of names, does she want to see everybody's fees on that paper?
Certainly not. So we ask for only what we need.
So instead of the star, we write the names of the columns we want.
SELECT first_name, surname, programme, FROM students.

The equals sign, for is exactly this.
Greater than, and less than. You know those signs from mathematics.

Less than or equal to, the same way.

AND is strict. OR is generous. NOT turns it around. That is all three.

Look at the brackets I am putting in.

Without the brackets, the computer would read it as: all Accounting students, OR Marketing students who owe money.
That is a completely different question, and you would lose the mark.
So when you mix AND and OR in one WHERE, put brackets around the OR part. Every time.

It means, is this value one of these? IN is just a tidy OR.

Run.
The console shows us the last query, so we are looking at the BETWEEN result.
Tanaka, Rudo and Chipo. One fifty, two hundred point five, and three twenty. All inside the range.

Now the last one, and this is the one that catches everybody, so pay attention.
Sometimes you need to find the records where something is missing.
The registrar says, which students have no date of birth captured? We must phone them.

Here is why. NULL does not mean a value. NULL means unknown.
And you cannot ask whether one unknown thing equals another unknown thing. The database cannot answer that.
So we write IS NULL instead.
WHERE date_of_birth IS NULL. Two words, no equals sign anywhere.
Run.
Memory Mpofu.
Her record went in without a date of birth, and now we have found her.
And the opposite is IS NOT NULL, for records where the field was filled in.

Four tools in this lesson, and the exam has a favourite way of asking for each one.
When the question says starting with, ending with, or containing, they want LIKE and a percent sign.
When the question lists two or three specific values, IN is the neat answer, but a chain of ORs also gets full marks.
When the question says between two numbers or between two dates, use BETWEEN, and remember both ends are included.

Let us see our five students first, so we know what we are starting with.

Line two. SET fees_paid equals two hundred and fifty. What am I changing it to?
Line three. WHERE student_id equals one. Who am I changing it for?
Which table, what change, and for whom. Three questions, three lines. Never forget the third one.
And notice I used student_id in the WHERE, not the name.
Why? Because student_id is the primary key, so I know for certain it can only be one person.

Now something clever, and this is a favourite exam question.
The college gives every IT student a fifty dollar bursary credit.
Now, I cannot write SET fees_paid equals fifty, because that would wipe out what they have already paid.
I want to add fifty to whatever is already there. Everybody's total is different.
So look at the SET line.
SET fees_paid equals fees_paid plus fifty.
Read that slowly. The new fees_paid equals the old fees_paid, plus fifty.
The column appears on both sides of the equals sign. That is not a mistake. That is exactly how you do arithmetic in SQL.
And the WHERE says programme equals NC IT, so it happens to a group, not to one person.
Run.

But understand what it would do.
With no WHERE clause, the database does not ask who. It assumes you mean everybody.
Every single student in the college would suddenly be doing NC IT. Farai in Accounting. Blessing in Marketing. All of them.
Five students here. But in a real college database, that is eight thousand records, destroyed in one keystroke.
And there is no undo. Only a backup can save you, and only if somebody made one.
So here is the habit I want you to build from today, and never break.
When you write UPDATE, type the WHERE clause first, before you type the SET.
Write the WHERE first. Then go back and fill in the SET. That way it is impossible to forget it.
Professionals do this. Now you know why.
The exam question sounds like this. Write an SQL statement to change the fees paid by student number one to two hundred and fifty dollars.

UPDATE students. SET fees_paid equals two fifty. WHERE student_id equals one. Semicolon.
And then there is a theory question that comes up again and again.
What is the effect of omitting the WHERE clause in an UPDATE statement?
Answer. All the records in the table will be updated, not just the intended ones.
One sentence, one mark, and now you will never forget it, because you have seen what it does.
Which table, what change, for whom. Three lines, every time.

The command is short, and that is exactly what makes it dangerous.

Notice something. There is no list of columns anywhere.
That is because DELETE always removes the entire row. You cannot delete just one field.
If you want to empty one field, that is not DELETE, that is UPDATE, setting it to NULL. Different job, different command.
Run.
Farai is gone.
Four students left. Tanaka, Rudo, Chipo, Blessing.
And notice the student numbers. One, two, four, five. There is a hole where three used to be.
That is correct behaviour, and it is important. The database will never reuse number three.
Because if it did, some old record somewhere pointing at student three would suddenly be pointing at a completely different person.
So the gap is not a bug. The gap is the database protecting your history.
DELETE takes any condition, exactly like SELECT does.
Same command, different WHERE.
DELETE FROM students WHERE fees_paid equals zero.
That means, remove every student who has not paid a single cent.
Run.
Look at that. Nothing was removed.
Still four students, exactly as before.
And that is a good lesson in itself. The only student with zero was Farai, and we already deleted him.
So the condition matched nobody, and the database did nothing at all. It did not complain, and it did not break.
A DELETE that matches nothing is not an error. It is just a quiet no.
Now, what if you want to empty a whole table, but keep the table itself?
There are two ways, and the exam wants you to know the difference.
The first way is DELETE FROM table_name, with no WHERE at all. That removes every row, one by one.
The second way is TRUNCATE TABLE table_name. That empties the whole table in one action.
Watch what I build here, so we do not touch our students.
A small table called temp_log, with two entries in it. Then I truncate it. Then I look at it.
Run.
Look at the result. The table is there, but it is empty.
The columns are still standing. log_id and message. But both entries are gone.
Now the exam difference, and write this down.
DELETE is DML. It removes rows one at a time, it can have a WHERE, and it can often be rolled back.
TRUNCATE is DDL. It removes all rows at once, it cannot have a WHERE, it is faster, and it resets the auto-increment counter back to one.
DELETE picks. TRUNCATE empties. That is the shortest way to remember it.
And now the third one, which we met in Chapter Two. DROP.
Our temp_log table is empty, but it is still standing there taking up space. Let us remove the table itself.
So watch. DROP TABLE temp_log.
And SHOW TABLES underneath, so we can see the proof.
Run.
Look at the list.
temp_log is not there any more. The table itself has stopped existing.
students is still there, safe, with our four learners inside.
Now here is the picture I want you to carry into the exam. Think of a filing cabinet drawer.
DELETE takes out the files you point at, and leaves the rest.
TRUNCATE empties the whole drawer, but the drawer is still in the cabinet.
DROP takes the drawer out of the cabinet and throws the drawer away.
Point at files. Empty the drawer. Throw the drawer away. Three commands, three pictures.
This comparison is asked so often that I want you to be able to write it in your sleep.
The question. Distinguish between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP.
DELETE. A DML command that removes selected records from a table, using a WHERE clause. The table structure remains.
TRUNCATE. A DDL command that removes all records from a table at once. The table structure remains, and the auto-increment counter is reset.
DROP. A DDL command that removes the entire table, including its structure and all its data.
Notice that each answer has two parts. What it removes, and what is left behind.
What it removes, and what is left behind. That is what the marker is looking for.
And one last thing before we leave this chapter, and it is the most important thing I will say all day.

Take your WHERE clause, put SELECT star FROM in front of it, and look at exactly which rows come back.
If those are the right rows, then change the word SELECT star FROM to DELETE FROM, and run it.
Test with SELECT, then destroy with DELETE. That one habit will protect you for your whole career.

Three definitions come out of this lesson, and they are worth easy marks.
One. What is a foreign key? A field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, used to link the two tables.
Two. What is referential integrity? A rule ensuring that a foreign key value must always refer to an existing record in the related table.
Three. What is data redundancy? The unnecessary repetition of the same data in a database, which wastes space and can lead to inconsistency.

Numbers.

Let us start with two tables only, students and enrolments, and add the third one afterwards.
Watch these four lines carefully. This is the shape of every join you will ever write.
Line one. SELECT, and the columns I want. And look how I write them.
students dot first_name. enrolments dot course_id. Table name, dot, column name.
Why the dot? Because both tables have a column called student_id, and the database must know which one you mean.
Line two. FROM students. That is my first table.
Line three. INNER JOIN enrolments. That is my second table.
Line four, and this is the heart of it. ON students dot student_id equals enrolments dot student_id.
The ON clause is the matching rule. It says, a row from here belongs with a row from there when these two numbers are the same.
That is the whole idea of a join. Find the rows that match, and put them side by side.

See the chain? Students link to enrolments. Enrolments link to courses.

Join questions carry big marks, and they are also where students freeze. So let me give you a recipe.
Step one. Read the question and write down which pieces of information they want.
Step two. For each piece, write down which table it lives in. Name, students. Course name, courses.
Step three. Ask, is there a table in the middle that links them? Usually yes.
Step four. Write FROM the first table, then INNER JOIN each other table, each one with its own ON.
Step five. Every ON is always primary key equals foreign key. Every single time.
Primary key equals foreign key. If you remember nothing else about joins, remember that.
And the definition question. What is a join? A join combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them.
One more warning. If you forget the ON clause completely, you do not get an error. You get every row matched with every row.

WHERE runs before the grouping. At that moment there are no groups yet, and there is no count yet.
You cannot filter on a count that has not been calculated. The database has not done the counting when WHERE runs.
So we need a filter that runs afterwards, once the piles have been counted.
So we use HAVING.
HAVING COUNT star greater than one.
HAVING is the WHERE clause for groups. That is the sentence to remember.
And it sits after the GROUP BY, never before it.

The question. Differentiate between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause.
Answer. WHERE filters individual records before they are grouped, and it cannot be used with aggregate functions.
HAVING filters groups after the grouping has taken place, and it is used with aggregate functions.
Before and after. Rows and groups. Those two contrasts are the marks.
And in a practical question, when you see the words for each, or per, that is your GROUP BY signal.
The number of students for each programme. Total sales per branch. Average mark per subject. All GROUP BY.
And when you see only those groups with, or where the count is more than, that is HAVING.
For each means GROUP BY. Only those groups means HAVING. Two phrases, two clauses.
Let me describe a problem you will meet in your first job.
You write a beautiful query. Three tables joined, a WHERE clause, sorted properly. It took you twenty minutes.
The next morning, the accounts clerk needs the same list. So you write it again for her.
The following week, the registrar needs it. And the head of department. And somebody in the library.
Now you have five copies of that query floating around the college, and one of them has a typing mistake in it.
The answer to this is a view.
A view is a saved query with a name on it. You write it once, and then everybody just uses the name.
And here is the definition for your exam. A view is a virtual table based on the result of a SELECT statement.
Say virtual. That word carries a mark, because it tells the marker you understand the next part.
A view does not store any data. It stores the question, not the answer.
So every single time somebody opens the view, the query runs again, on the data as it is at that moment.
A view is never out of date. That is the whole beauty of it.
The command is CREATE VIEW, and it is easier than you expect, because you already know the hard part.
So watch the first line.
CREATE VIEW paid_up_students AS.
That word AS is doing the joining. It says, this name means the query that follows.
And then underneath it, an ordinary SELECT. Nothing special at all.
The students who have paid more than one hundred dollars.
That is the pattern for every view you will ever write. CREATE VIEW, a name, AS, and then any SELECT.
Run.
Now look. It says it succeeded, but there is no list of students.
And that is exactly right. We have not asked a question yet. We have only saved one.
The view is now sitting in the database with a name, waiting for somebody to use it.
Now here is the part that makes it worth it.

Look at that. I am treating it exactly like a table. Same command, same shape, no difference.

And if a student pays tomorrow morning, she will appear in this view automatically, with nobody changing anything.
Because the view stores the question, not the answer. Remember that.
You can also put a WHERE on top of a view, or an ORDER BY, exactly as you would with a table. It behaves like a table in every way.
Before we drop it, let me give you the three reasons views exist, because the exam asks for them.
One. Simplicity. A complicated join becomes a simple name that anybody can use.
Two. Security. And this is the big one.
You can give a clerk access to a view that shows only names and programmes, and no fees at all.
She can do her work, and she can never see the money column, because it is not in the view.
Three. Consistency. Everybody in the college is using the same definition of a paid up student. One definition, one truth.
And to remove one, it is DROP VIEW.
DROP VIEW paid_up_students. And SHOW TABLES underneath, to see what is left.
Run.
The view is gone.
But look carefully. Our students table is still there, with all five students inside it.
Nothing was lost, and I want you to understand why that is guaranteed.
Dropping a view only throws away a saved question. The data was never inside the view in the first place.

The theory. Define a view and state two advantages of using views.
A view is a virtual table whose contents are defined by a SELECT statement. It does not store data itself.
Advantage one, it simplifies complex queries for the end user. Advantage two, it improves security by hiding columns the user should not see.
The practical. Create a view called something, showing certain fields, for certain records.
CREATE VIEW, the name, AS, then the SELECT with its WHERE. Semicolon at the very end, not after the view name.
And one they slip in to catch you. Does a view store data?
No. A view stores the SELECT statement, and it runs it fresh each time the view is accessed.
No, it stores the query. Nine words, one mark.
Before we write any commands, let me set the scene, because this chapter is really about trust.
In a college database, who should be able to change a student's final mark?
Not the librarian. Not the accounts clerk. Not the student. Only the examinations officer.
But all of those people need to open the same database every day to do their jobs.
So the database must be able to tell them apart. Every person gets their own username and password.
And then each username is given only the powers it needs. Nothing more.
That idea has a name, and it is worth knowing. The principle of least privilege.
Give every user the smallest set of permissions that still lets them do their job.
The family of commands for this is DCL, Data Control Language, which we met all the way back in Chapter One.
Now, I must tell you honestly: none of these commands will run in this practice console.
This console is a small database living inside your browser. It has no logins and no passwords, so there is nobody to grant anything to.
On a real MySQL server, in XAMPP or at work, they all work exactly as I am about to show you.
So for these next steps, read the code, copy it into your notes, and understand every word. They are examinable.
First we make the user exist. Look at the editor.
CREATE USER, then the username in single quotes, then the at sign, then localhost in single quotes.
Now what is that at localhost part? It confuses everybody the first time.
It says where this person is allowed to connect from. localhost means, only from this same machine.
So even if somebody in another country steals the password, they cannot use it, because they are not sitting at that machine.
That is a real security control, and it is the kind of detail that earns you extra marks.
Then IDENTIFIED BY, and the password in single quotes.
Notice the password is written in plain text in the command, but MySQL stores it scrambled. It is never kept as plain text on the disk.
Now, at this moment, the accounts clerk exists. She has a username and a password.
But she can do absolutely nothing. She can log in and stare at an empty screen.
Creating a user gives them zero powers. Every single power must be given deliberately. That is by design.
Now we give her the powers she needs. The command is GRANT.
And the shape is always the same. GRANT what, ON where, TO whom.
What, where, whom. Three words, and you can write any GRANT statement in the exam.
Read the first one with me.
GRANT SELECT, INSERT. Those are the what. She may look at records, and she may add records.
ON college_db dot students. That is the where. Only that one table, in that one database.
TO accounts_clerk at localhost. That is the whom.
And notice what she did not get. No UPDATE, and no DELETE.
So she can register a new student, and she can look up any student, but she can never change or remove a record.
That is the principle of least privilege, written in one line of SQL.
Now look at the second statement, for the head of department.
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON college_db dot star.
ALL PRIVILEGES means every power. And the star after the database name means every table in that database.
So the head of department can do anything, to anything, inside college_db.
Be careful with that one. Give ALL PRIVILEGES to as few people as possible.
The privileges you must be able to name are SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and ALL PRIVILEGES.
And when somebody changes job, or leaves, you must be able to take the powers back.
That command is REVOKE, and it is GRANT in reverse.
Look at the shape.
REVOKE what, ON where, FROM whom.
And there is the one difference to watch. GRANT uses the word TO. REVOKE uses the word FROM.
GRANT to. REVOKE from. Students lose marks by mixing those two little words, so say it a few times.
Here we are taking away her INSERT permission. She may still look, but she may no longer add new students.
And notice her SELECT permission is untouched. REVOKE only removes exactly what you name.
At the bottom I have written DROP USER as a comment.
That removes the account altogether, and you would use it the day somebody leaves the college for good.
Revoke when their duties change. Drop the user when the person leaves.

First. State two DCL commands and explain their use.
GRANT gives specified privileges on a database object to a user. REVOKE withdraws privileges that were previously granted.
Second. Write a statement to allow the user clerk to view records in the students table.
GRANT SELECT ON college_db dot students TO clerk at localhost, semicolon.
Third, and this one is a favourite. State three ways of securing a database.
One, creating individual user accounts with strong passwords. Two, granting only the minimum privileges each user needs. Three, using views to hide sensitive columns.
And you can add a fourth if you want the extra mark. Taking regular backups, so the data can be restored after a failure or an attack.
Remember the shapes. GRANT what, ON where, TO whom. REVOKE what, ON where, FROM whom.

Because the paper does not say, write a SELECT with a WHERE. It says something in English, and you must translate it.
So here is the method. Four steps, and I want you to use them on every single question.
Step one. Read the question twice. Twice, not once. The second reading is where you catch the word not, or the word each.
Step two. Underline what they want to see. Names? Totals? Everything? That becomes your SELECT line.
Step three. Underline the conditions. The words who, whose, with, more than, starting with. Those become your WHERE line.
Step four. Look for the signal words that point at a clause.
For each, or per, means GROUP BY. Sorted, or in order of, means ORDER BY.
Top three, or first five, means ORDER BY plus LIMIT. Including those who have none means LEFT JOIN.
Underline. Translate. Then write. Never start writing before you have underlined.

Number one. The missing semicolon. It costs a mark and it takes one second to fix. Go back and check every answer for it.
Number two. Quotes on numbers, or no quotes on text. Text in quotes, numbers bare. Check every value.
Number three. A comma after the last column in a CREATE TABLE. Look at the last line before the closing bracket.
Number four. Writing the clauses in the wrong order. ORDER BY before WHERE will never work.
Number five. Forgetting the WHERE in an UPDATE or a DELETE. In the exam that is marks. At work it is your job.

Number seven. Spelling the column name differently from the way it was created. student_id is not studentid.
